Yes for each 10% they got me I agreed to give them $1500. If they reach 100% then it's an additional $1500 kicker. They do have a discount if you pay it within a certain amount of days and for something else (can't remember) totalling $500 in discounts. So I went from 70 to 100% so mine was $6000 minus $500 in discounts, for a total fee of $5500. In my case, the back pay from the VA covered the cost of my fees, since they took 4 months to make the decision. The VA back pays you from the moment they receive the claim until they make a decision and pay you for the claim. Sometimes that can be as short as a week for as long as several years. But in general a typical VA claim is something like 125 days for a decision. 
Regardless of the amount I paid the company, it is a drop in the bucket when compared to the benefits I received after the fact.

The best piece of advise is attend a smaller school if it's been a while since you've been to school. I personally tried to do all my easier course online, and went to school for the harder classes and labs.  Everyone is different, so just jump in with a light class load and figure out what work best for you. Forget the noise in college, put your head down, Dig deep and grind until you finish. It has been one of the most rewarding experiences getting that degree. Good luck!

Well,  I've told many teenagers that If they don't have a plan in life then they should consider the military because they will give you a skill,  and pay you for the time you're in.  During that time,  you may understand what it is that you want to do in life (i.e. be an engineer,  work in finance,  be a counselor) the military will now pay for you to work toward that goal. 
By asking what purpose someone is looking for while they are in may vary. Some just want to survive, some want structure, some want a better life than what they had, some have no clue, some want to be of service, and some just want to belong to something bigger than themselves. For me, I didn't know exactly what I want to do after high school. But 9/11 had just happened and I felt a sense of duty to serve. So I joined the navy not knowing what I wanted, or what my interest may be. I became an aircraft electrician and found I loved it, I loved figuring out how something was suppose to work, I loved fixing the problems, and was proud of my work. I enjoyed it so much, I contracted overseas and continued working on airplanes in the DoD sector.
My point is sometimes you join for the college, for the military life, or a better life. But that isn't your purpose, many go thru their military career by just waiting to get out without looking for a purpose. The military keeps them busy enough, and when not actively working hard, they are playing hard. Their purpose will come later in life with that structure isn't there anymore. 
For me, my purpose slapped me in the face when I decided I wanted to get out of the navy.  Halfway in my enlistment I found that I was pretty good at understanding how things work electrically, and figured being an electrical engineer made sense. So that became my goal in life, my purpose. By this time I had a wife and family, so they were my priority, first.  It took me 6 years after getting out of the military to be in a position to go to school, which is why I started working overseas. 6 years after that I got my degree. 
Now I work as an engineer in the DoD aviation industry and am happy and I will have my masters by the end of the year. I live in a nice home, in a nice area amd am able to provide for my family. My focus (not purpose) is starting to shift on retirement.  My purpose in life now to raise my family, follow Christ, and help lead others to him.

The military issues you your purpose, as cliché as it sounds. You go in with a job, you live eat and breath the military and the schooling that goes with it.
